map.An Axiom City episode — Lessons 6-1 & 6-: An Axiom City episode. Lessons 6-1 & 6-2 in one go. It has three reader gates. Solve the math to move the story.
map.Pattern distortion below the library, cr: A glitch is under the library, crew. It is small and teal. And it is very rude.
map.Previously: on a rained-out field day, t: Last time: it rained on field day. The crew woke VEX. VEX is a piece of Ada Vex's Pattern Engine. Since then, the city's signs have turned to scribbles. Last night, the trail led to Vexhall Library.
map.Vexhall Library, after closing. The reci: Vexhall Library, at night. Its cards hold the fix-it formulas. Now the cards are torn to bits.
map.It shredded every recipe card into fract: It tore each recipe card into fraction pieces. Half a card here. A quarter of a card there…
map.Those cards hold the formulas that FIX t: Those cards hold the formulas that FIX the signs. It ate the steps!
map.Distortion source: Ada's cipher vault, u: The glitch comes from Ada's code vault. It is under this floor. Its first ring opens only to right quotients. Those are division answers. Bring tape. Bring brains.
map.Beneath the library. A brass door. One r: Under the library. A brass door. One ring of twelve notches. It hums and glows.
map.Repair plan. This spool holds 3 metres o: The plan. This spool holds 3 metres of ribbon. Each fixed stack of card pieces needs a strip. Each strip is one quarter of a metre long.
So the door is asking 3 ÷ 1/4. How many quarter-metre strips fit in three metres? An old vault trick.
map.Definitions loaded: the piece-size you d: Words loaded. The piece-size you divide BY is the divisor. The answer you get from division is the quotient. Draw a bar for each metre. Cut each metre into quarter-metre pieces. Count the pieces. Bars do not lie.
map.Dividing by a fraction asks: how many of: Dividing by a fraction asks: how many of that piece fit inside? Say the divisor is smaller than 1. Then more than one piece fits in each whole. So the quotient can be bigger than the start.
map.Reader — you're our fifth crew member. S: Reader, you are our fifth crew member. Set the first notch. Cut the ribbon. Then split the paste!
Andre's ribbon is 3 metres long. Each card stack needs a strip just 1/4 metre long. Cut up the bar model. How many strips can the crew cut? Then split the paste below.
map.Layla's glow-paste: 2/3 of a jar, shared: Layla's glow-paste: 2/3 of a jar. It is shared the same among 4 repair benches. How much paste does each bench get?
map.Conceptual: dividing by a fraction asks: Conceptual: dividing by a fraction asks this. How many of that piece FIT INSIDE the whole? The divisor (1/4 metre) is smaller than one metre. So each metre holds more than one strip.
map.Procedural: use the bar model. Slice ONE: Procedural: use the bar model. Cut ONE metre into quarter-metre strips. Count them. Then keep counting, metre by metre, across all three. For the paste: 2/3 of a jar is shared the same among 4 benches. Each bench gets one fourth OF those two-thirds. Cut those shaded parts into four same rows. Read one row.
map.KLUNK. A taped-up card slides out of a w: KLUNK. A taped-up card slides out of the wall. The glitch hisses at it from up top.
map.2¼ is a mixed number — a whole number an: 2¼ is a mixed number. It is a whole number plus a fraction. Write it as one fraction. Then it is not scary.
map.Shortcut loaded: to divide by a fraction: Shortcut: to divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal. That is the flipped fraction. ÷ ¾ becomes × 4/3, because ¾ × 4/3 = 1. Flip the divisor. Never flip the start amount.
map.Two roads, one quotient: count the piece: Two roads, one quotient. Count the pieces in a bar model. Or flip the divisor and multiply by the reciprocal. Both must match. That is your built-in check.
map.Reader — the second notch wants batches: Reader, the second notch wants batches and tape. Mix it and measure it!
map.The restored card: the jar holds 2¼ cups: The fixed card: the jar holds 2¼ cups of glow-paste. One batch uses ¾ cup. Lock A: how many batches can the crew mix? Lock B: Mateo's tape is 1½ metres. Each card spine needs ¼ metre. How many spines can he tape?
map.Conceptual: a mixed number is a whole nu: Conceptual: a mixed number: a whole number plus a fraction. Write it as ONE fraction first. Then divide. Dividing by a fraction equals multiplying by its reciprocal. That is the flipped fraction.
map.Procedural: make the pieces match. Turn: Procedural: make the pieces match. Turn 2¼ cups into quarter-cups. Turn ¾ cup into quarter-cups. Then count how many batch-size groups fit. For the tape, dividing by ¼ is multiplying by 4/1. That is the reciprocal of 1/4.
map.The ring clicks again. The glitch panics: The ring clicks again. The glitch gets scared. It starts to scribble on the vault wall.
map.Nice try. We just divided 1½ by ¼ and go: Nice try. We just divided 1½ by ¼. We got SIX. We split by a small piece. The answer GREW.
map.It's lying to guard the inner lock. Boss: It lies to guard the inner lock. Boss rule one: bosses lie.
map.The divisor's size decides everything. D: The divisor's size decides it all. Divide by a number bigger than 1 → the quotient shrinks. Divide by a fraction smaller than 1 → the quotient grows. The glitch bets you won't check.
map.VEX projects a demo board on the vault d: VEX shows a test board on the vault door. Time to get ready to fight back.
map.So every answer carries its own receipt:: So each answer comes with a receipt. Multiply the quotient by the divisor. You must land back on the start.
map.Eighteen third-metre pieces rebuild six: Eighteen third-metre pieces make six whole metres. The glitch can't argue with a receipt.
map.Always run the receipt: quotient × divis: Always check the receipt: quotient × divisor = the amount you started with. If it does not match, the division is wrong. It does not matter how sure the glitch sounds.
map.The inner ring. Three locks. The glitch: The inner ring. Three locks. The glitch puffs up to twice its size. It is still quite small.
Reader, three locks, one lying glitch. Do the divisions. Then find the counterexample. It will break the lie in half.
Split the quotients. Split the glitch.
map.Boss Gate ahead: two quotients to comput: Boss Gate next. Find two quotients. Break one lie with one counterexample.
map.BOSS GATE. Three locks. One lying glitch: BOSS GATE. Three locks. One lying glitch. (You can do this. Maybe. Yes.)
map.The inner ring. Three locks stand betwee: The inner ring. Three locks stand before one lying glitch:
map.The glitch scrawled: \"Dividing ALWAYS m: The glitch wrote a lie. Pick the result that proves it wrong: "Dividing ALWAYS makes things smaller!"
map.Conceptual: the divisor's size decides t: Conceptual: the divisor's size decides what the quotient does. Divide by a fraction SMALLER than 1. The quotient gets BIGGER than the start. Small pieces fit many times. Dividing by a number bigger than 1 makes it smaller.
map.Procedural: flip each divisor into its r: Procedural: flip each divisor into its reciprocal. Then multiply. ÷ 2/5 becomes × 5/2. For ÷ 1¼, write 1¼ as 5/4 first. Then × 4/5. For the lie-lock, find a division. Its quotient must be BIGGER than its start.
map.The ring split it into harmless sparks!: The ring broke it into sparks! They can't hurt us. And look, the cards tape THEMSELVES back up.
map.Quotients verified. First ring: open. Li: Quotients checked. First ring: open. The library signs fix their own spelling right now.
map.One ring down. But the sparks flew DEEPE: One ring down. But the sparks flew DEEPER into the vault. They went to a door with tiny raised numbers…
map.New distortion humming. It speaks in pow: A new glitch hums. It speaks in powers. To be continued…
map.Quotient & divisor.The divisor is the pi: Quotient & divisor.The divisor is the piece-size you divide by. The quotient is the answer. "3 ÷ 1/4" asks how many quarter-metre strips fit in 3 metres. A bar model shows each piece.
map.Mixed numbers & the reciprocal.Rewrite a: Mixed numbers & the reciprocal.Write a mixed number as one fraction. Then multiply by the divisor's reciprocal. That is the flipped fraction. ÷ ¾ becomes × 4/3.
map.Dividing can grow.Divide by a fraction s: Dividing can grow.Divide by a fraction smaller than 1. The quotient is BIGGER than the start. Check any quotient with its receipt: quotient × divisor = the start amount.
map.\"A lock that only opens to a correct qu: "This lock opens only to a right quotient. That is not mean. It is just very, very honest." — A.V.
map.completed Unit 6 · Episode 1: Split the: did Unit 6 · Episode 1: Split the Glitch. You can divide fractions and mixed numbers.
map.Thank you for reading with the crew. Epi: Thank you for reading with the crew. Episode 2 hums behind the power ring.
map.Different shelf, same idea: Ms. Ortiz's: New shelf, same idea. Ms. Ortiz has 6 metres of string. Each tag needs a 1/3-metre piece. Ask it as a fit question: how many 1/3s fit inside 6?
map.Bar model: draw 6 one-metre bars. Slice: Bar model: draw 6 one-metre bars. Cut each metre into thirds. Each metre holds 3 third-metre pieces.
map.Count all the pieces: 6 metres × 3 piece: Count all the pieces: 6 metres × 3 pieces per metre = 18 pieces. Receipt: 18 × 1/3 = 6. The quotient times the divisor gives back the start.
map.Your turn — same idea, different numbers: Your turn. Same idea, new numbers:
map.A 5-metre cord cut into 1/2-metre pieces: A 5-metre cord is cut into 1/2-metre pieces. How many pieces?
map.Different card, same moves: 1¾ cups of s: New card, same moves. 1¾ cups of syrup. Each glaze uses ½ cup. Write the mixed number first: 1¾ = 7/4.
map.Sense check: three whole glazes and half: Does it make sense? Three whole glazes and half of one more. Receipt: 3½ × ½ = 1¾. It gives back the start. So the quotient is good.
map.Demo lock: 2 jars of ink, and each stamp: Test lock: 2 jars of ink. Each stamp pad uses 2/5 of a jar. Flip the divisor: 2 ÷ 2/5 = 2 × 5/2.
map.2 × 5/2 = 5 stamp pads. Notice: the quot: 2 × 5/2 = 5 stamp pads. Look: the quotient (5) is BIGGER than the start (2). Each share is smaller than a whole jar.
map.Receipt: 5 × 2/5 = 2. Quotient × divisor: Receipt: 5 × 2/5 = 2. Quotient × divisor = the start. Every time. Even when the quotient grew.
map.Type a strip count first — the bar model: Type a strip count first. The bar model will shade as you go.
map.That's 3/4 of a METRE — you took one qua: That is 3/4 of a METRE. You took one quarter OF the ribbon. The lock asks: how many quarter-metre strips FIT INSIDE 3 metres? Count the small boxes.
map.The ring buzzes. Shade the bar model: ho: The ring buzzes. Shade the bar model. How many quarter-metre boxes fill ONE metre? Keep counting across all three metres.
map.Ribbon sliced! Now split the paste — pic: Ribbon cut! Now split the paste. Pick how much each bench gets.
map.6 jars?! Sharing among 4 benches can't g: 6 jars?! 4 benches share it. No bench can get MORE paste than there is. Sharing splits the amount. Each share is smaller than 2/3.
map.8/3 jars means you MULTIPLIED by 4. Shar: 8/3 jars means you MULTIPLIED by 4. Sharing among 4 benches divides. Each bench gets one fourth OF the 2/3 jar.
map.So close — that's one fourth of one THIR: So close. That is one fourth of one THIRD. The benches share two thirds. Cut both shaded thirds into 4 rows. Count what one row holds.
map.Lock 1 turns! 12 quarter-metre strips fi: Lock 1 turns! 12 quarter-metre strips fit in 3 metres (12 × 1/4 m = 3 m). And 2/3 ÷ 4 = 1/6 of a jar per bench. The first notch clicks in.
map.The card waits. Fill in both locks — bat: The card waits. Fill in both locks. Batches first. Then spines.
map.Lock A jams — that's 2¼ × ¾. You multipl: Lock A jams. That is 2¼ × ¾. You multiplied BY the divisor. To divide by ¾, flip it. Multiply by 4/3 instead.
map.Lock A holds. Rewrite 2¼ as one fraction: Lock A holds. Write 2¼ as one fraction made of quarters. Then ask how many ¾-cup groups fit inside it. Or flip ¾ and multiply.
map.Lock B jams — that's 1½ × ¼. Don't shrin: Lock B jams. That is 1½ × ¼. Don't shrink the tape! Dividing by ¼ asks how many quarter-metres FIT. So multiply by the reciprocal, 4/1.
map.Lock B holds. 1½ is a mixed number — rew: Lock B holds. 1½ is a mixed number. Write it as halves or quarters first. Then count quarter-metre pieces. Or multiply by 4.
map.Lock 2 turns! 2¼ ÷ ¾ = 3 full batches, a: Lock 2 turns! 2¼ ÷ ¾ = 3 full batches. And 1½ ÷ ¼ = 6 taped spines. The receipts check: 3 × ¾ = 2¼ and 6 × ¼ = 1½. The glitch looks scared.
map.Lock 1 first — how many 2/5-jar servings: Lock 1 first. How many 2/5-jar shares fit in 4 jars?
map.Lock 1 jams — that's 4 × 2/5. You multip: Lock 1 jams. That is 4 × 2/5. You multiplied by the divisor. Flip it. Dividing by 2/5 means multiplying by 5/2.
map.Lock 1 holds. Each jar holds two and a h: Lock 1 holds. Each jar holds two and a half shares of 2/5. Or just flip the divisor: 4 × 5/2.
map.Lock 1 open! Now Lock 2 — how many 1¼-me: Lock 1 is open! Now Lock 2. How many 1¼-metre drawer fronts come from 3¾ metres?
map.Lock 2 jams — that's 3¾ × 1¼. Don't mult: Lock 2 jams. That is 3¾ × 1¼. Do not multiply the board by the divisor. Write both mixed numbers as quarters. Then divide.
map.Lock 2 holds. Rewrite 3¾ and 1¼ as quart: Lock 2 holds. Write 3¾ and 1¼ as quarters. Now the pieces match. Then count how many drawer fronts fit.
map.Two locks open! Lock 3: pick the result: Two locks open! Lock 3: pick the result that BREAKS the glitch's lie.
map.Lock 3 holds. 10 ÷ 2 = 5 SHRANK — that r: Lock 3 holds. 10 ÷ 2 = 5 got SMALLER. That helps the lie. It does not break it. Find a division whose answer GREW.
map.Lock 3 holds. 4 × 2/5 is a MULTIPLICATIO: Lock 3 holds. 4 × 2/5 is a MULTIPLICATION. The lie is about dividing. Beat it with a division.
map.Lock 3 holds. 3¾ ÷ 1¼ = 3 is true, but 3: Lock 3 holds. 3¾ ÷ 1¼ = 3 is true. But 3 is SMALLER than 3¾. The glitch just smirks. Pick the quotient that got bigger than its start.
map.ALL LOCKS OPEN. 4 ÷ 2/5 = 10 scorches, 3: ALL LOCKS OPEN. 4 ÷ 2/5 = 10 scorches. 3¾ ÷ 1¼ = 3 drawer fronts. And 4 ÷ 2/5 = 10 is the counterexample. The quotient GREW. So dividing does not always shrink. The lie snaps. The ring spins. The glitch breaks into sparks!
Yes! Now go back and open that gate.
map.Walk the steps above again — you've got: Go over the steps above again. You can do this.
